results.title: Using class weights with loss function for train/val/test splits - PyTorch Forums
results.content: Because of the data pipeline (which I don’t really want to go back and totally rewrite) the balance of classes is different between the train, validation, and test sets. My feeling is that, I do need to have a separate instance for the validation set because I don’t want them weighted based on the training set class distribution, but I shouldn’t use any class weights because the validation set should be a proxy for the test set……within which I wouldn’t know the class distribution. If your train-valid split was stratified, then you shouldn’t have to redo the class weights during validation, as the relative abundances of classes in training set and validation set are similar to the full dataset (Which is atleast what I do for my classification tasks). For example, in binary classification, if one of the classes is naturally rarer than the other and the total dataset (train + valid) represents the abundance of the rarer class in the “wild“ then using class-weights calculated from the full dataset makes sense (to me).

results.content: # What are best practices around combining train/val/test splits when training a production model? Say I'm training a deep neural network and I have split my data into train, val, and test splits. I have trained many models on the train data and then using the val data during the training loop for things like ReduceLRonPlateau and early stopping. Then, I would like to use the hyperparameters I used in my best model to train a production model and I would like to use as much of the data as I can. One option would be to combine all the data into one set and train it using the learning rate schedule that my previous ReduceLRonPlateau produced and stopping it at the same number of epochs. Another option would be to combine the train and test sets and then use the val set again for ReduceLRonPlateau and early stopping. If you use the test set for model selection, it is no longer a test set -- it is another validation set. I would recommend you select models based on validation loss and leave the test set to be used only as a final estimate of out of sample performance. > One option would be to combine all the data into one set and train it using the learning rate schedule that my previous ReduceLRonPlateau produced and stopping it at the same number of epochs. In this case, we can assume that all the images are in a single folder, and we are to divide the images into 3 folders, ‘train’, ‘val’, and ‘test’. The above code randomly chooses a number of files and moves them to the ‘train’ folder. Then it randomly chooses a number of files and moves them to the ‘val’ folder. Then finally, it moves the remaining files to the ‘test’ folder. Now, as we are dealing with a segmentation task here, we also need to move the segmentation masks with the same filename to the respective folders, as well. ### Now, what if the image folder contains class subfolders? As is generally the case in datasets like CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, etc. We can do that by recursively iterating over the files in each sub-folder of the image directory and moving them to either of ‘train’, ‘val’, or ‘test’ folders. results.title: How to Define Effective Validation Acceptance Criteria
results.content: # How to Define Effective Validation Acceptance Criteria. Effective **validation acceptance criteria** must be **SMART**: Specific to requirements, Measurable with clear pass/fail thresholds, Achievable within resources, Relevant to quality and safety, and Time-bound. + 7.1 When Should Acceptance Criteria Be Finalized in the Validation Cycle? + 7.3 Who Should Be Involved in Developing Validation Acceptance Criteria? + 7.4 Can Acceptance Criteria Differ Between Validation Phases? + 7.5 How Do You Handle Acceptance Criteria Deviations During Validation? * Align acceptance criteria with regulatory requirements and industry-specific guidelines for compliance. When maneuvering through **validation procedures** in regulated industries, you’ll need to grasp the complex web of **regulatory requirements** that govern **acceptance criteria**. When you thoroughly understand the regulatory foundation, you’ll develop criteria that satisfy authorities while meaningfully validating your systems and processes. Beyond simply meeting regulatory requirements, establishing effective validation criteria for medical products demands a structured approach. Risk-based approaches to **validation criteria** development enable you to allocate resources where they matter most—to areas with the highest potential impact on **patient safety** and product efficacy. By conducting thorough risk assessments before defining **acceptance criteria**, you’ll establish appropriate **validation requirements** proportionate to identified risks. * Critical quality attributes that directly affect product safety require stringent acceptance criteria with minimal allowable deviation. Your criteria should be specific enough that different testers would reach identical pass/fail conclusions when evaluating the same test results—eliminating ambiguity and creating an auditable validation framework. ### When Should Acceptance Criteria Be Finalized in the Validation Cycle? You should finalize acceptance criteria during early validation stages. ### Who Should Be Involved in Developing Validation Acceptance Criteria? Document your criteria thoroughly, ensuring all participants sign off on final validation requirements. ### Can Acceptance Criteria Differ Between Validation Phases? Yes, your acceptance criteria can differ between validation phases. You’ll need stricter criteria during qualification phases and more operational-focused criteria during process validation, reflecting different validation phase requirements. ### How Do You Handle Acceptance Criteria Deviations During Validation? Effective acceptance criteria management requires validation process adjustments through change control procedures when issues arise during testing. As you develop **validation acceptance criteria**, guarantee they’re clearly defined, measurable, and aligned with regulatory requirements.
